Item 1.01. Entry into a Material Definitive Agreement.
On November 9, 2026, Moderna, Inc. (the “Company”) entered into Amendment No. 1 (the “Amendment”) to its Credit and Guaranty Agreement, dated as of November 19, 2025 (the “Credit Agreement”), among the Company, as borrower, the guarantor subsidiaries from time to time party thereto, the lenders from time to time party thereto and Ares Capital Corporation, as administrative agent and collateral agent. The Amendment was entered into by the Company, Ares Capital Corporation and the lenders party thereto and became effective on November 9, 2026.
The Amendment reduces the applicable interest rate margins for the initial term loans and delayed draw term loans by 0.75 percentage points, from 5.50% to 4.75% per annum for loans bearing interest at a forward-looking term rate derived from the Secured Overnight Funding Rate and from 4.50% to 3.75% per annum for loans bearing interest based on the base rate. The Amendment also extends the maturity date for those loans from November 24, 2030 to November 24, 2031.
The Amendment extends the availability period for the first $400 million of delayed draw term loan commitments from November 24, 2027 to November 24, 2029 and for the remaining $500 million of delayed draw term loan commitments from November 24, 2028 to November 24, 2029, in each case, subject to earlier termination in accordance with the Credit Agreement. Borrowings of delayed draw term loans remain subject to the applicable conditions under the Credit Agreement. Except as modified by the Amendment, the Credit Agreement remains in effect, including its guarantees and collateral security.
The above summary of the Amendment does not purport to be complete and is qualified in its entirety by reference to the full text of the Amendment, a copy of which is filed as Exhibit 10.1 to this Current Report on Form 8-K and is incorporated herein by reference.

Aon Completes Acquisition of USI to Establish the Premier U.S. Middle-Market Platform

DUBLIN, November 16, 2026 - Aon plc (NYSE: AON), a leading global
professional services firm, today announced that it has completed the acquisition of USI, a leading provider of property and casualty, employee benefit, personal risk and retirement solutions for the middle market, for a total purchase price of
$17.0 billion. 
The acquisition establishes the premier platform in the large and growing U.S. middle-market segment, building on the success of
Aon’s acquisition of NFP in 2024. It also expands the firm’s direct access to the Excess & Surplus (E&S) segment and extends its Risk Capital and Human Capital capabilities to provide better choice, superior solutions and
greater value for clients. Additionally, the combination enhances Aon’s industry-leading data platform to generate richer insights and deliver differentiated, AI-enabled solutions to serve rising client
needs. 
“Today marks an important step forward for our clients, colleagues and shareholders as we welcome USI to the Aon family and formally
establish the premier U.S. middle-market platform,” said Greg Case, CEO of Aon. “We could not be more excited to work with USI’s team members and together with colleagues across Aon and NFP set a new standard of capability,
expertise and client service.” 
Case added: “Businesses of every size, across every industry and region face growing and interconnected risk
and people issues. At Aon, we have built a differentiated, one-firm operating model that is converting insight into innovation, and innovation into growth for our clients. With this combination now complete,
we are even better positioned to bring essential decision-making tools and solutions to our U.S. middle market clients, allowing them to address their risks, build resilience and drive better outcomes.” 
The addition of USI – the tenth largest U.S. insurance broker with approximately $3 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,500 team members
across nearly 200 U.S. offices – substantially enhances Aon’s presence in the large and growing middle-market segment. Effective immediately, USI will go to market as “USI, an Aon company,” under the leadership of Mike
Sicard, who now serves as President of Aon and global CEO of the middle market across Aon, NFP and USI. 
“With Aon’s distinctive capabilities
and integrated, one-firm platform, we are entering an exciting new chapter for our colleagues and clients,” said Sicard. “We are thrilled to join with our Aon and NFP colleagues to bring the best
of our capabilities to every relationship, create greater value for our clients and unlock more opportunities for our teams.”

early 2027. The company also intends to provide regular updates on its progress toward achieving the $395 million of expected net adjusted EBITDA synergies it identified as part of the acquisition. 
Advisors 
BofA Securities and Citi served as financial
advisors to Aon on the transaction. Cravath, Swaine & Moore LLP acted as legal counsel to Aon, McDermott Will & Schulte LLP acted as legal advisor to Aon with respect to regulatory matters and Skadden, Arps, Slate,
Meagher & Flom acted as financing counsel to Aon.

USI, an Aon company, is one of the largest insurance brokerage and consulting firms in the United States, delivering property and casualty,
employee benefits, personal risk, program, wholesale and retirement solutions to its clients nationwide. Headquartered in Valhalla, New York, USI has become a premier insurance brokerage and consulting firm by leveraging the USI ONE Advantage®, an interactive platform that integrates proprietary and innovative client solutions, networked local resources and enterprise-wide collaboration to deliver customized results with positive,

Cheniere Announces Promotion of Zach Davis to President and Chief Financial Officer 
HOUSTON—(BUSINESSWIRE)— Cheniere Energy, Inc. (“Cheniere” or the “Company”) (NYSE: LNG) announced today the promotion of
Zach Davis to President and Chief Financial Officer from Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, effective November 12, 2026. Mr. Davis will continue to report to Jack Fusco, Cheniere’s Chairman and Chief Executive
Officer. 
“Zach’s leadership in developing and executing Cheniere’s financial framework has been fundamental to Cheniere’s
transformation into a global energy leader,” said Mr. Fusco. “This promotion recognizes Zach’s strategic management and executive leadership and reflects the Board’s confidence in his ability to build on Cheniere’s
momentum as we embark on our next chapter of growth.” 
Mr. Davis said, “I am grateful to Jack and the Board of Directors for the
confidence and trust they have placed in me, and I am excited to take on broader responsibilities as we continue to execute on our long-term strategy at Cheniere.” 
Mr. Davis has served as Chief Financial Officer of Cheniere since August 2020 and also serves as a director and Chief Financial Officer of the general
partner of Cheniere Energy Partners, L.P. (NYSE: CQP). Mr. Davis joined Cheniere in November 2013 and previously served as Senior Vice President, Finance and Vice President, Finance and Planning. Mr. Davis has over 20 years of experience,
primarily in energy and infrastructure finance. 
About Cheniere 
Cheniere Energy, Inc. is the leading producer and exporter of LNG in the United States, reliably providing a clean, secure, and affordable solution to the

Diamondback Energy, Inc. Announces Core
Midland Basin Acquisition
MIDLAND, Texas, Nov. 16, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE)
-- Diamondback Energy, Inc. (NASDAQ: FANG) (“Diamondback” or “the Company”) today announced that it has entered
into a definitive purchase agreement to acquire certain subsidiaries of Double Eagle IV Midco, LLC and Double Eagle V Midco, LLC (together
“Double Eagle”) in exchange for approximately 15.56 million shares of Diamondback common stock and $2.15 billion of cash,
subject to customary adjustments (the “Double Eagle Acquisition”). The cash portion of this transaction is expected to be
funded through a combination of cash on hand, borrowings under the Company’s credit facility and/or proceeds from term loans.
“This acquisition is another important step
in Diamondback’s continued growth within the Midland Basin. The undeveloped inventory acquired in this transaction significantly
increases the operated working interest and net present value of high return projects that we were already going to drill, while also
adding more undeveloped inventory to our portfolio throughout the Midland Basin,” stated Kaes Van’t Hof, Chief Executive Officer
and Director of Diamondback.
Mr. Van’t Hof continued, “In
2022, as Diamondback gained subsurface understanding of the emerging Barnett zone in the Midland Basin, we decided to combine that understanding
with the differentiated land expertise of the Double Eagle team. Today’s deal is the culmination of that successful partnership,
with Diamondback buying out the 40% of the partnership we did not already own, known as ‘netting up’ in the oil business.
Our confidence in both the quality of the resource and our execution cost structure ahead of large-scale development made this the right
time to complete this transaction. Importantly, Diamondback does not need to add a rig or materially alter our development plan as a result
of this transaction, ensuring a seamless integration.”
Mr. Van’t Hof continued, “We
are also excited to announce early results from our first full-section Barnett development in Spanish Trail in Midland County. At a recent
peak, this project, consisting of four 10,000-foot lateral wells, produced approximately 7.5 MBo/d and 37 MMcf/d, exceeding internal expectations
for full-field development and in line with delineation wells in the area. These early results further validate our geologic understanding
of the play and provide momentum as we execute full-field Barnett development in 2027 and for years to come.”
Cody Campbell and John Sellers, Co-Chief Executive
Officers of Double Eagle, commented, “We are pleased to once again partner with Diamondback on this transaction. These assets offer
high-quality inventory and meaningful Barnett runway, and we are confident they will be in great hands with an operator that shares our
commitment to West Texas. We are proud of what the Double Eagle team has built in the Midland Basin and plan to continue our operating
momentum with our multi-rig development program on our remaining assets in Reagan County.”

Opening Remarks 
 Chairman Kevin Warsh 
At the Productivity and Jobs Task Force Conference, hosted by the Federal Reserve Board and the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, San Francisco, California 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Mary, thank you, and welcome. 
I'm grateful to Mary and her colleagues for helping to arrange this gathering. This is my very first visit to a Reserve Bank as Chairman. I wouldn't call it a snap inspection, but I'm certainly impressed. Everything I see reflects high expectations and the inquiring, forward-looking spirit that we need in the Federal Reserve System. 
It's good to have Fed colleagues with us from around the country. Central banking is a team sport, and I'm pleased you're here. This conference is an expression of the mission we all serve: One Fed. Fit for Purpose. Focused on the Future. 
I also want to thank Marc, Chad, and Asha for leading our Productivity and Jobs Task Force. You're giving the scarcest of resources—your time and your commitment. It's a service to the Fed and to our nation, and I'm grateful. 
This task force is one of five I have convened as Chairman. These groups are a way of broadening our thinking . . . of inviting robust discussions that take us further and deeper than fleeting data points or daily market moves. Our task forces are an intellectual investment to better equip us for the next policy conjuncture and beyond. 
The common attributes of Asha, Marc, and Chad, the reason I asked them to lead, is not just their exceptional insight and experience. It's their battlefield bravery in the world of ideas . . . their intellect and their willingness to think hard about what might happen next. They, in turn, asked me to open the task force discussion to a wide cross section of stakeholders—and that's the purpose of this conference. 
As for me, I always feel energized to be in this part of California. I arrived here way back in 1988 as a Stanford undergrad. I remember sitting in Green Library over Thanksgiving break during my freshman year, reading and wrestling with great works from a canon that I had scarcely known existed, beginning my initiation into the world of ideas. It was a special time to be in the Bay Area—neither boom nor bust, a quieter period between tech surges. And, today, just as I was then, I'm keen to listen to and learn from the great people and first-rate minds around me. 
The current era may be the most transformational period in my adult lifetime, marked by the arrival of the general-purpose technology called "super intelligence." SI is an entirely new force in economic life and society. It demands our special attention. 
Even a few years ago, the idea that we could have, in our pockets, instant access to genius-level intelligence on almost any subject would have seemed far fetched. Today, with the advances of SI, it's happening. The marginal cost of satisfying limitless curiosity—on questions large and small—is falling fast, perhaps even trending toward zero. 
In the tradition of endogenous growth theory in economics, ideas are the ultimate resource. If living standards are to advance, conditions must be favorable to the generation of new ideas. It should be no surprise, then, that the United States is leading. Societies that bring forth the best ideas tend to prosper most. The implications for economic policy can hardly be overstated. 
While an idea can be costly to discover, it's free to use. And because an idea is nonrival—that is, one person's use doesn't diminish anyone else's—its value grows with the number of people who use it. The Nobel laureate Paul Romer, among others, has shown that a doubling of ideas and other key inputs can more than double output, allowing increasing returns to scale.1 
Even so, in the U.S. over the past several decades, breakthrough ideas have been harder to find. By some estimates, research efforts have increased more than 20 times since the 1930s. Yet, as Nick Bloom, Chad Jones, and their coauthors have pointed out, "Research productivity has fallen by an even larger amount."2 The result: Productivity growth has fluctuated, and in recent quarters, it's been reasonably strong. But it hasn't yet broken out definitively and structurally to the upside. 
Long-run growth, I should note, is also a function of the rate of increase in the number of people producing new ideas and setting them in motion. The conventional view holds that as population growth slows, there may be fewer new ideas to drive prosperity.3 The increasing challenge of generating breakthrough ideas, combined with slower population growth, helps explain why many in the economics profession, in the post-crisis environment, returned to the theme of secular stagnation. 
Does super intelligence dramatically change this picture? Well, there are certainly some indications that it does. 
SI might be somewhat different from general-purpose technologies of the past, such as the internal combustion engine or electricity. Those inventions made for decades of follow-on innovation but did not themselves automate the creation of ideas. What might set SI apart, as an economic influence, is that it could supercharge idea generation. It appears to be changing the method—and the speed—of innovation. If idea generation broadens, growth could be sustained at a level substantially higher than the long-run average.4 
For all of that, however, humans should not be underestimated. There is no replacing the minds and the hands of men and women. Machines that can amass or even exceed human knowledge are still machines. They do not take the place of human judgment, morality, or responsibility. Humans are the designers and the builders, and humans must be the deciders. 
For our country in this era, consider how much is on the line. I remember Bob Mundell, another Nobel recipient, saying years ago that the most important fact of the twentieth century was the rise of the United States as a superpower.5 For us today, that is more than a fact of history—it is a charge to keep. And so we must ask, can you be a superpower without super intelligence? 
My Fed colleagues and I are not at this conference as futurists to speculate on each new turn technology might take. And we're certainly not here to make predictions. We can't know the future and ought not to pretend otherwise. 
Our job is to prepare for whatever comes next. That means contingency planning, which becomes only more important when the world is changing this fast. Our aim today is a humble one: to ask the right questions. 
As policymakers, we have to be mindful that great opportunities rarely come risk free. And the risks in this case, if overlooked, can be highly disruptive and economically costly. SI empowers all, including bad actors, so we are thinking especially of critical infrastructures and their potential vulnerabilities. 
And, of course, I think of economic policy in the era of SI. At the Fed, our role in all this is neither advocacy nor opposition. Our responsibility is to recognize that the widespread adoption of this technology will have significant impact on the economy, with important implications for monetary policy down the road. 
The big questions are about magnitude, scope, and timing. Will this new technology deliver a rise in total factor productivity? Will the democratization of specialized knowledge significantly raise standards of living? When will the surge start, and when will it taper? Will it happen sooner and faster here than in other countries? Will adversaries race to deploy SI, intending to do harm to our economy? 
The answers will matter greatly—and that is why we're thinking about them now, in a sober and serious way. I expect much more clarity with the passing of time. 
Still, it's worth considering the range of economic outcomes we could see over the next several years, depending on how SI progresses. The Board's staff has begun to evaluate various contingencies, applying stylized, model-based frameworks to generate scenarios. 
These are illustrative scenarios, not forecasts. Moreover, many other outcomes—probably including one that will prove most accurate—could be drawn. Consider them a starting point for the very useful discussions we've got lined up for today. 
At one end, SI leads to an increase in productivity and economic gains that are shared broadly across labor and the owners of capital. In that event, real GDP growth rises persistently above its long-run average, and the U.S. stays close to full employment. 
Other outcomes, however, could be less positive. An SI-driven expansion could bring substantial labor market disruption as some jobs are displaced, rather than complemented, by technology. GDP growth would still rise above its long-term average. But widespread automation, combined with labor market frictions, could push the jobless rate above levels consistent with full employment. 
Or SI could disappoint. After significant capital investment and stock market gains, expected returns could turn down and equity valuations could fall, leading to an economic slowdown and a more notable rise in unemployment. In time, the economy would recover, but without the productivity gains. 
I stress that while I'm not here to offer predictions, I'm not exactly impartial about American leadership in a time so filled with both challenge and possibility. 
I thought back recently to my days at the Hoover Institution and to a collaboration with my fine mentor and colleague John Cogan. As we wrote some years ago: "If we meet the challenges before us, America has a bright future with strong, durable economic growth, abundant economic opportunities, vibrant and secure communities, and a healthy environment. Future generations will inherit a dynamic economy capable of delivering technological advancements that will extend lives and promote human flourishing."6 
That is the goal, the ultimate scenario, that all of us here hope to see. It's a privilege to be a policymaker at a time of such consequence—and it's an encouraging sign to be in the company of so many serious and capable men and women. 
Thank you all very much.

CONTRIBUTION
Smart supervision for small banks
Contribution by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, for Börsen-Zeitung
Frankfurt am Main, 16 November 2026
Germany’s small and regional banks are trusted partners to the Mittelstand and households across the country, often drawing on deep-rooted relationships in their communities. They play an important role in financing the real economy and support jobs and investment in the regions they serve.
This reflects a broader European reality. Across Europe, a diverse banking sector – combining a range of business models, sizes and areas of expertise – helps ensure that households and businesses can access the financing they need. 
As Europe searches for ways to strengthen its long-term growth and competitiveness, these banks will continue to play an important role. But they are very different from large, internationally active banking groups: their business models are often simpler, their activities more focused and their risk profiles less complex. A regulatory and supervisory framework that recognises those differences can support both resilience and competitiveness.
This is already partly the case. The EU prudential framework recognises the diversity of EU banks through the concept of proportionality: the idea that regulatory requirements and supervisory practices should reflect a bank’s size, complexity and risk profile, while maintaining high standards that protect depositors and the stability of our financial system. 
This framework already covers a large share of Europe’s smaller banks. Today, around 75% of the banks supervised by national authorities in the euro area – more than 1,400 institutions – qualify as small and non-complex, and thus benefit from proportionate treatment. In Germany, that share is even higher: 81%. Among other things, these banks need only report up to 30% of the data reported by their larger counterparts. Supervisors also tailor the frequency and intensity of their oversight to the complexity and risk profile of each bank. 
At the same time, experience gained from applying the framework over recent years has shown that some smaller banks still face regulatory requirements and supervisory practices that were originally designed with much larger and more complex institutions in mind. A more tailored approach would allow supervisors to focus on the risks that matter most while reducing unnecessary complexity for banks.
Over recent months, the ECB and national supervisors have examined where oversight can be simplified without compromising resilience. The result is a set of practical proposals aimed at making oversight for smaller banks more risk-focused, efficient and effective. Rather than creating a new framework, the proposals build on the one already in place for small and non-complex banks. The goal is simple: to preserve the same high standards of safety and soundness while reducing unnecessary complexity.
One important step would be to broaden the range of institutions eligible for the existing framework. To qualify today, a bank must have a balance sheet of less than €5 billion. But experience has shown that size alone does not necessarily make a bank more complex. In Germany, for example, a wave of consolidation among smaller and regional banks has created larger institutions without necessarily making their business models riskier or more complex. In fact, greater scale can help these banks benefit from lower cost-to-income ratios, become more efficient and invest in key areas like digitalisation and cybersecurity. 
Amending the regulation to allow national authorities to raise the threshold to €10 billion, where warranted by the bank’s risk profile and the structure of its domestic banking sector, would therefore enable more banks to benefit from proportionate treatment.
Another key change would be to redefine what “non-complex” actually means. Today, some banks are excluded from the framework for largely technical reasons related to resolution planning, rather than reasons of genuine complexity.
Together, these regulatory changes would bring an additional 150 or so banks under the small and non-complex umbrella, making them eligible for more proportionate treatment.
But changing legislation is only one part of the solution. We also need to adapt the way supervision is carried out in practice, and we are already working to do just that.
For banks whose risk profile is stable and well understood, some supervisory exercises could be carried out less frequently or more efficiently. For example, supervisors could increasingly run stress test projections centrally rather than requiring banks to carry them out themselves. This would substantially lighten the workload for almost 1,000 institutions that currently need to do so. Reporting requirements are another area that could be simplified. To this end, together with the European Banking Authority we are pursuing reforms that should ultimately reduce reporting by small and non-complex banks to around 5% of the data points reported by large banks. This would allow both supervisors and banks to focus their efforts where risks are greatest, while reducing unnecessary burdens.
None of this changes a fundamental reality: smaller banks are not immune to risk.
Cyber threats are becoming more sophisticated. Geopolitical tensions create uncertainty. Digitalisation is transforming the financial sector. Climate and nature-related risks are increasingly affecting businesses and households, and the banks that finance them.
That is why greater proportionality cannot mean lower standards. Depositors in a small regional bank should have the same confidence in the safety of their savings as customers of a large international institution. That principle is paramount when considering changes to the framework for small and non-complex banks.
A stronger and more competitive Europe needs banks that make the most of their strengths. And across the continent, there is growing recognition that competitiveness and resilience go hand in hand. Well-designed regulation should support both.
For smaller banks, that means oversight that preserves high standards while recognising their specific characteristics. A more proportionate framework can help them remain resilient, direct scarce resources towards managing the risks that matter most, and focus on what they do best: helping local businesses and hidden champions thrive.

Bank of Canada Governor Tiff Macklem to step down in June 2027
FOR IMMEDIATE RELEASE
 Media Relations
Ottawa, Ontario
November 16, 2026
 Share this page on Facebook 
 Share this page on X 
 Share this page on LinkedIn 
 Share this page by email 
The Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada announced today that Governor Tiff Macklem has informed them that he will not seek a second term as Governor when his seven-year term expires on June 2, 2027. The Board has begun a search process to select the next Governor of the Bank. 
“It has been the highlight of my career to serve as the 10th Governor of the Bank of Canada,” Governor Macklem said. “My time as Governor has seen Canada navigate a more fragmented, shock-prone world. The Bank has faced these challenges by acting decisively, by using sound judgment in the face of uncertainty, and by serving Canadians with humility and a steadfast commitment to its mandate.” 
The Governor thanked the Board of Directors of the Bank of Canada, the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister for entrusting him with the stewardship of Canada’s central bank. “It is a privilege to serve as Governor, and I remain fully committed to fulfilling my responsibilities and delivering for Canadians through the remainder of my term,” he said. 
Additional Information 
The following is the process leading to the appointment of a new Governor: 
The independent directors on the Bank’s Board of Directors have formed a Search Committee with a mandate to undertake a recruitment process for the selection of the next Governor. 
The Search Committee will be assisted by executive recruiting firm Egon Zehnder. Interested candidates are encouraged to review the Executive Brief for the role and contact Egon Zehnder confidentially to discuss their candidacy at BoCgovernor-gouverneurBdC@egonzehnder.com 
The recruitment process is expected to be completed by spring 2027. 
Subject to the approval of the Minister of Finance and the federal Cabinet, the independent directors of the Board will appoint the next Governor for a seven-year term beginning June 3, 2027.

Some Potential Financial Stability Implications of Artificial Intelligence 
 Governor Michael S. Barr 
At the Seventh Annual Association for Computing Machinery International Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Finance, Milan, Italy 
 Share 
 Watch Live 
Thank you for the opportunity to speak to you today.1 This is the fourth speech I have given in the past year devoted exclusively to artificial intelligence (AI), and most of the others have also addressed it in some way. The effects of AI on people and economies around the globe are among the most important issues we are facing today. 
Let me stipulate at the outset that I am an optimist about the long-term promise of AI to empower individuals, businesses, and institutions across society. I remain hopeful that if we manage today's challenges and tomorrow's potential disruptions forcefully and effectively, that AI will lift up people, make them more productive, and broadly raise living standards—that most people will learn more and earn more. One of the reasons I'm optimistic about this technology is that I'm also optimistic about the capacity of society to understand and respond to the changes that AI will bring—to engage in a constructive dialogue about ensuring that the benefits from AI are not overwhelmed by the disruptions it will inevitably bring and the risks it may pose. 
This conference is part of that dialogue, directed at questions that I believe will be crucial in ensuring that AI is a positive force in the financial system that empowers individuals to better manage their finances and access credit and services, lowers costs and enhances the capabilities of financial service providers, and also makes markets function more effectively. But AI can only succeed in strengthening our financial system in this way if it also supports financial stability, something that is indispensable to a healthy economy. 
As has been the case for some time, there are important insights about AI and financial stability in the Federal Reserve's latest Financial Stability Report (FSR) issued on Friday. This edition of the twice-yearly report focuses on the AI investment boom and research by the Fed's staff to assess the degree of leverage in some of the innovative debt structures being employed to finance this growth. I will recap the report's findings and then turn to a discussion of what economic research can tell us about the benefits and risks of integrating AI into financial markets, focusing on wholesale trading. Next, I will examine the potential benefits and risks of AI's effect on cybersecurity and then finally consider what AI might mean for consumer and investor protection. 
The AI Investment Boom
Anyone watching the news or their retirement plans these past couple of weeks is aware of the questions that investors have raised about the sustainability of the AI investment boom. I should issue the usual disclaimer here that policymakers on the Federal Reserve Board do not target levels of financial markets. Markets go up, and markets go down, and I assiduously avoid commenting on the ups and downs in markets. We do assess longer-term issues that relate to financial stability, and the latest FSR covers several. 
In a previous speech, I discussed three different scenarios summarizing the wide range of possible outcomes for how much AI could alter the economy.2 In one possible scenario among several, even if AI turns out to be a transformative innovation that vastly improves productivity, a key question is whether investors will see returns on the AI buildout on a timeline and to an extent consistent with their expectations or whether a different outcome could lead to a significant repricing. The potential investment losses that could result from a large-scale repricing could lower output growth in two ways: first, from the direct effect of a drop in investment, which is a component of gross domestic product; and, second, from the knock-on effects of this loss of wealth in lowering consumer and potentially business spending. As discussed in the latest FSR, the equity premium, a rough measure of the additional return that investors require for holding stocks relative to risk-free bonds, is at low levels relative to historical norms, though not nearly as low as the levels reached during the dot-com stock market boom.3 This is just one indicator to assess where broad measures of equity valuations are relative to historical norms. 
Leverage in the Data Center Buildout
In addition to the question of equity valuations, the AI buildout has been increasingly funded by debt. The Federal Reserve's FSR delves into three ways in which the financing of AI data centers and related investments, which it calls "advanced computing debt," could affect financial stability: (1) the rapid growth of this debt, (2) circular financing networks, and (3) other complex financial obligations. In the case of a significant repricing of AI investments, stress from these three aspects of AI financing could amplify the repricing of AI investments. 
On-balance-sheet debt of the seven largest AI firms has been growing significantly in 2026 and is expected to exceed $800 billion before year's end. The growth of debt at these firms brings to mind the growth of debt in the telecom investment cycle of the late 1990s and early 2000s. The FSR compares hyperscaler firms' cumulative capital spending and debt issuance since 2020 with those of all firms in the telecommunications industry during the broadband investment cycle that started in 1995. While the hyperscalers have yet to surpass their comparators of the earlier boom, the recent acceleration in their capital expenditures suggests they may do so soon.4 
While these firms' on-balance-sheet debt levels have grown substantially, their other obligations, such as long-term contracts, lease commitments, and residual value guarantees, have grown even more rapidly. The FSR estimates that the potential maximum nominal value of these types of obligations, or off-balance-sheet liabilities, now exceeds $3 trillion.5 A significant share of these obligations results from complex arrangements in which hyperscalers and other large firms with strong credit ratings indirectly support the financing of projects that involve other firms with weaker credit, or provide support for public utility investments. These off-balance-sheet liabilities include obligations relating to energy supply contracts, long-term data center and compute leases, and a wide variety of off-balance-sheet financing structures. As I have discussed in previous speeches, this financial complexity can be opaque to unsophisticated investors, and that opacity can exacerbate selloffs when investor sentiment shifts, as it is hard to know where risk resides. As a result, the development of these substantial off-balance-sheet structures warrants close monitoring. Perhaps just as important, in addition to the hyperscalers, lower-credit-quality firms most dependent on external funding have seen their cost of capital rise significantly in recent months and, as a result, are turning to more complex asset-backed financings. 
In addition, the hyperscaler firms and large graphics processing unit (GPU) producers also have over $100 billion in cumulative equity investments in large language model (LLM) labs and cloud-computing start-ups. These equity investments represent a form of "circular financing" in which hyperscaler firms and GPU makers invest capital in smaller firms, and the smaller firms turn around and use these funds to rent or purchase GPUs and compute from the firm that made the investment. These investments represent a relatively small share of the hyperscalers' and GPU producers' balance sheets, but they are critical for the smaller firms receiving the investments. For the AI buildout investments to ultimately become economically viable, the smaller firms will eventually have to replace that funding from their suppliers, the hyperscalers and GPU makers, with revenue from paying customers. 
Another indirect form of circular financing in which the hyperscalers and GPU producers support purchases of their products and services is the use of collateral guarantees for asset-based financings. As the firms most dependent on external financing bump up against financing constraints, they shift from issuing corporate bonds to issuing asset-based financing. To support the credit of these financings, the larger higher-credit firms often guarantee the resale value for the data centers or GPUs that are used as collateral to back the financings. These guarantees, or collateral backstops, are reported as off-balance-sheet liabilities because they represent the degree to which hyperscalers and GPU producers might absorb losses in the event of defaults and collateral liquidation. 
As we take a step back and consider the enormous scope of AI-related investment in capital stock, it is helpful to consider how it compares to that for previous technology cycles. By one estimate, the capital investment associated with the AI buildout could plausibly rival or even exceed the investments associated with previous infrastructure investment booms, including those associated with railroads in the 1870s, highways in the 1950s and '60s, and fiber-optic cable in the 1990s.6 Each of these investment booms may have felt overbuilt at some point, but today we are glad to have the railroad, highway, and fiber-optic capacity that they put in place. Some of those earlier booms fizzled, with consequences for the broader financial system. Given the still-limited amount of debt backing the current boom, I'm less concerned about direct losses. However, with leverage at hedge funds and broader risk appetite apparently quite high, a sharp reversal could lead to rapid deleveraging and, potentially, self-reinforcing fire sales. Further, the leverage used in equity strategies has also increased in recent years. This leverage is provided, in part, via the prime brokerage services of large dealers. Thus, while the high levels of capital at the largest banks provide a bulwark against spillovers, counterparty exposures could rise in a period of equity market volatility, so it's important to keep monitoring exposures, including exposures to counterparties that have taken large positions in AI. 
Moreover, the bulk of a data center's cost comes from the GPUs and other specialized chips used in AI. One concern is that these specialized chips may depreciate quickly as newer technologies overtake them, such that the capacity they represent will not be of much use in the future. Currently, the lease rates of older vintages of chips appear to be holding up, suggesting that there are uses even for computing technology behind the cutting

Boris Vujčić
Vice-President of the European Central Bank 
SPEECH
Risks and resilience in the euro area financial system
Keynote speech by Boris Vujčić, Vice-President of the ECB, at the Euro Finance Week
Frankfurt am Main, 16 November 2026
It is my great pleasure to open this year's Frankfurt Euro Finance Week. This event provides a timely opportunity to reflect on the state of the euro area financial system and the challenges ahead. It also comes just two days before the ECB publishes its latest Financial Stability Review (FSR). My key message today is that Europe needs more market-based finance. At the same time, however, a larger role for non-banks must go hand in hand with stronger system-wide safeguards.
While most risks identified in the FSR have been on our radar for quite some time, two stand out very prominently compared to the situation a year ago. These relate to developments in artificial intelligence (AI) and sovereign debt markets.
In our assessment a year ago, AI-related vulnerabilities were fundamentally associated with stretched valuations in global stock markets and the risk that market sentiment could shift abruptly. At present however, while the risk of market repricing, rather than abating, has further increased, AI-related risks to system-wide stability now stem from a range of additional factors – the expansion of external funding from equity to debt markets, concentration of exposures, quickening AI adoption and potential cyberattacks.
In fact, rapid advances in AI models’ cyber capabilities raise risks that have systemic implications. So too does the high concentration of third-party providers of critical services (notably of information and communications technology systems) on which euro area banks and financial intermediaries rely. An early-release FSR special feature published today explores this further.
Concerns about sovereign debt sustainability have been present throughout recent years, reflecting elevated public debt levels and persistently weak fiscal fundamentals in some euro area countries. Sovereign debt fragilities have further increased on both sides of the Atlantic, and are among the factors driving up long-term yields. The risk of global spillovers has also increased. Risks are compounded by inflation concerns, a notable rise in debt issuance by hyperscalers, growing government financing needs, a more price-sensitive investor base, heightened policy and geopolitical uncertainty, and longer-term structural challenges.
Turning to economic activity, over the past year, the euro area economy has proven remarkably resilient in the face of multiple challenges. Economic growth continued to expand in the third quarter of this year, although less dynamically than in the previous quarter.
But the ongoing war in the Middle East continues to push energy prices up, leading to high energy inflation. At the same time, trade policy uncertainty has not abated significantly. Headline inflation in the euro area increased to 4% in October, from 3.8% in September, mainly due to higher energy prices. Underlying inflation has remained broadly stable and wages are not showing a material response at this stage. Overall, recent energy price developments may push inflation higher, while weaker confidence and rising borrowing costs should partially contain this by weighing on growth.
The adverse impact of the energy shock on economic growth has been partly offset by an upbeat AI narrative. But the market correction following the US mid-term elections earlier this month, although contained, serves as a reminder to remain cautious about AI valuations.
Key risks to stability of the euro area financial system
Three developments and related sources of risk and vulnerability for euro area financial stability stand out.
First, artificial intelligence. The rapid expansion of AI is creating new challenges for financial stability. Growing debt and equity exposures to AI-linked firms are raising concerns about market concentration, overly optimistic earnings expectations and potential credit risks.
The scale of firms’ financing needs across the AI supply chain is unprecedented. Large cloud and AI infrastructure providers are increasingly turning to debt markets, with issuance volumes reaching record highs this year. Borrowing is likely to increase further, as cumulative capital expenditure by major US technology firms is projected to reach USD 5.5 trillion by 2030.
At the same time, firms are increasingly relying on opaque off-balance-sheet financing structures and circular financial arrangements to fund AI infrastructure investment. For example, chipmakers and cloud providers may invest in AI labs that, in turn, commit to purchasing their hardware and services.
Equity issuance is also surging, with IPO volumes now on track to exceed the dot-com bubble high, relative to US GDP. Historically, such surges have often coincided with market peaks, pointing to the risk of excessive investor optimism. This is concerning given that, while current market valuations rest on expectations of extraordinary earnings growth, the outlook remains highly uncertain.
Undoubtedly, the growing adoption of AI across the financial sector offers significant opportunities for efficiency gains. But it also introduces new vulnerabilities, including greater dependence on a small number of technology providers and heightened cyber and operational risks.
In particular, increasingly capable and autonomous AI systems are magnifying the scale, speed and sophistication of cyberattacks. Social engineering attacks are also becoming more effective. At least in the near term, this may shift the balance in favour of attackers, as financial institutions may face higher costs and greater constraints in deploying AI for defence. 
In response, ECB Banking Supervision has called on banks to strengthen their cyber defences, accelerate efforts to address vulnerabilities, and adapt their risk management frameworks to the rapidly evolving threat of cyberattacks.
The second development relates to fiscal pressures. A challenging fiscal outlook could test investor confidence and lead to a repricing of sovereign risk. Sovereign debt levels are elevated in several euro area countries and major advanced economies, where growing concerns about debt sustainability have already led to a sharp rise in long-term sovereign yields. In the euro area specifically, higher borrowing costs and structural headwinds that hinder potential growth could further strain fiscal positions and rekindle concerns in highly indebted countries. 
Higher issuance needs and a shift toward a more price-sensitive investor base also add to sovereign risks. The ability of the investor base to absorb additional supply will be key to ensuring the orderly functioning of sovereign bond markets. Hedge funds have become a significant but procyclical source of liquidity, while large Japanese investors may further reduce euro area government bond holdings if Japanese yields rise. At the same time, the substantial financing needs associated with the AI investment boom raise questions about potential competition for capital between public and private borrowers, including whether AI-related debt issuance could put upward pressure on financing costs or crowd out other investment.
The third development concerns the non-bank financial sector. The steadily growing share of non-bank financial intermediation offers opportunities to diversify sources of financing and support economic growth. While banks remain closely interconnected with the non-bank financial sector, the structural transformation of the financial system is changing how shocks are transmitted and amplified.
Private credit and private equity funds are playing an increasingly important role in financing the build-out of AI infrastructure, adding to concerns about leverage, opacity and interconnectedness across the financial system. 
Euro area investment funds have significantly increased their exposures to AI in recent years, through both equities and debt securities. A reassessment of the AI narrative may trigger an abrupt repricing in markets and significant valuation losses. This could lead to a surge in investment fund redemptions, increasing the risk of forced asset sales, with the interplay of rising portfolio concentration and leverage potentially amplifying market stress.
The growing footprint of leveraged hedge funds in sovereign bond markets creates additional vulnerabilities. 
Risks in the non-bank financial sector are thus closely linked to developments in AI and sovereign debt markets. The potential for these risks to materialise simultaneously could lead to losses and liquidity pressures in one market spilling over into others, amplifying risks to financial stability.
Enhancing resilience in the non-bank financial sector
Against a backdrop of geopolitical headwinds and elevated financial stability risks, preserving the resilience of the euro area banking sector remains essential. Banks have maintained strong capital and liquidity positions, supported by solid profitability and retained earnings. Current regulatory capital buffers do not appear to be a binding constraint on lending. Instead, they provide important safeguards and should be preserved as insurance against future shocks. 
The picture of resilience is more mixed across the non-bank financial sector.
Non-bank and market-based finance is playing an increasingly important role in financing the euro area economy, which is a welcome development. Deeper and more integrated European capital markets can broaden financing opportunities for firms, support investment and improve risk-sharing across the financial system. Advancing the savings and investments union is an important priority for Economic and Monetary Union.
But as non-bank financial intermediation grows, we also need to ensure that the policy framework keeps pace with the risks. While the banking sector is subject to a well-established macroprudential framework, the tools available to address systemic risks in the non-bank financial sector remain limited. Without enhanced EU-level supervision and a system-wide approach to non-bank finance, vulnerabilities may build up in the sector, amplifying market-wide shocks and potentially spilling over to the banking sector.
Of course, non-bank finance is highly diverse, and risks are not evenly distributed across institutions and business models. Our main concern is with the activities and intermediaries that contribute to the build-up of systemic vulnerabilities, particularly through excessive leverage, liquidity mismatches and interconnectedness with banks.
Leveraged trading strategies in core financial markets, including sovereign bond and repo markets, can support market liquidity in normal times. But a rapid unwinding of these positions during periods of stress can amplify that stress and disrupt markets that are normally very liquid.
Similarly, private credit can diversify financing sources for firms. While risks currently appear contained, the rapid growth of private credit warrants close monitoring, given limited transparency, growing interconnectedness with banks and insurers, and potential liquidity mismatches.
These developments underscore the need to strengthen the policy frameworks for non-banks and enhance their resilience to system-wide shocks.
For investment funds, this means addressing structural liquidity mismatches by better aligning redemption terms with the liquidity of underlying assets.

Technical Note
Brief Explanation of the CPI
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) measures the change in prices paid by consumers for goods and services. The CPI reflects
spending patterns for each of two population groups: all urban consumers and urban wage earners and clerical workers.
The all urban consumer group represents over 90 percent of the total U.S. population. It is based on the expenditures
of almost all residents of urban or metropolitan areas, including professionals, the self-employed, the poor, the
unemployed, and retired people, as well as urban wage earners and clerical workers. Not included in the CPI are the
spending patterns of people living in rural nonmetropolitan areas, farming families, people in the Armed Forces, and
those in institutions, such as prisons and mental hospitals. Consumer inflation for all urban consumers is measured by
two indexes, namely, the Consumer Price Index for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U) and the Chained Consumer Price Index for
All Urban Consumers (C-CPI-U). 
The Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W) is based on the expenditures of households
included in the CPI-U definition that meet two requirements: more than one-half of the household's income must come
from clerical or wage occupations, and at least one of the household's earners must have been employed for at least 37
weeks during the previous 12 months. The CPI-W population represents approximately 30 percent of the total U.S.
population and is a subset of the CPI-U population.
The CPIs are based on prices of food, clothing, shelter, fuels, transportation, doctors' and dentists' services, drugs,
and other goods and services that people buy for day-to-day living. Prices are collected each month in 75 urban areas
across the country from about 6,000 housing units and approximately 22,000 retail establishments (department stores,
supermarkets, hospitals, and other types of stores and service establishments). All taxes directly associated with the
purchase and use of items are included in the index. Prices of fuels and a few other items are obtained every month in
all 75 locations. Prices of most other commodities and services are collected every month in the three largest
geographic areas and every other month in other areas. Prices of most goods and services are obtained by personal
visit, telephone call, web, or app collection by the Bureau's trained representatives.
In calculating the index, price changes for the various items in each location are aggregated using weights, which
represent their importance in the spending of the appropriate population group. Local data are then combined to obtain
a U.S. city average. For the CPI-U and CPI-W, separate indexes are also published by size of city, by region of the
country, for cross-classifications of regions and population-size classes, and for 23 selected local areas. Area
indexes do not measure differences in the level of prices among cities; they only measure the average change in prices
for each area since the base period. For the C-CPI-U, data are issued only at the national level. The CPI-U and CPI-W
are considered final when released, but the C-CPI-U is issued in preliminary form and subject to three subsequent
quarterly revisions.

 THE EMPLOYMENT SITUATION - OCTOBER 2026 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, and the unemployment rate changed 
little at 4.1 percent, the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Employment increased in 
professional and business services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. 
This news release presents statistics from two monthly surveys. The household survey measures labor 
force status, including unemployment, by demographic characteristics. The establishment survey 
measures nonfarm employment, hours, and earnings by industry. For more information about the 
concepts and statistical methodology used in these two surveys, see the Technical Note. 
Household Survey Data 
Both the unemployment rate, at 4.1 percent, and the number of unemployed people, at 7.1 million, 
changed little in October. The unemployment rate has remained in a narrow range of 4.1 percent to 
4.3 percent since March. (See table A-1.) 
Among the major worker groups, the unemployment rates showed little or no change in October for 
adult men (3.9 percent), adult women (3.6 percent), teenagers (13.9 percent), and people who are 
White (3.7 percent), Black (6.6 percent), Asian (2.8 percent), or Hispanic (4.7 percent). (See 
tables A-1, A-2, and A-3.) 
The number of long-term unemployed (those jobless for 27 weeks or more), at 2.0 million, changed 
little over the month. The long-term unemployed accounted for 27.6 percent of all unemployed 
people. (See table A-12.) 
Both the labor force participation rate, at 61.9 percent, and the employment-population ratio, at 
59.3 percent, changed little in October. These measures have shown little net change since January. 
(See table A-1.) 
The number of people employed part time for economic reasons increased by 339,000 to 4.8 million in 
October. These individuals would have preferred full-time employment but were working part time 
because their hours had been reduced or they were unable to find full-time jobs. (See table A-8.) 
In October, the number of people not in the labor force who currently want a job changed little at 
6.0 million. These individuals were not counted as unemployed because they were not actively 
looking for work during the 4 weeks preceding the survey or were unavailable to take a job. (See 
table A-1.) 
Among those not in the labor force who wanted a job, the number of people marginally attached to 
the labor force changed little at 1.6 million in October. These individuals wanted and were 
available for work and had looked for a job sometime in the prior 12 months but had not looked for 
work in the 4 weeks preceding the survey. The number of discouraged workers, a subset of the 
marginally attached who believed that no jobs were available for them, also changed little over 
the month at 448,000. (See Summary table A.) 
Establishment Survey Data 
Total nonfarm payroll employment rose by 165,000 in October, higher than the average monthly gain 
of 48,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment increased in professional and business 
services, in health care, and in transportation and warehousing. (See table B-1.) 
Employment in professional and business services increased by 70,000 in October, well above the 
average monthly gain of 15,000 over the prior 12 months. In October, employment continued to trend 
up in professional, scientific, and technical services (+33,000), in administrative and support and 
waste management and remediation services (+28,000), and in management of companies and enterprises 
(+9,000). Professional and business services has added 269,000 jobs since a recent low in October 
2025. 
Health care added 42,000 jobs in October, higher than the average monthly gain of 31,000 over the 
prior 12 months. In October, employment gains occurred in hospitals (+16,000), home health care 
services (+11,000), and outpatient care centers (+5,000). 
In October, transportation and warehousing added 25,000 jobs, reflecting growth in couriers and 
messengers (+17,000) and air transportation (+4,000). Transportation and warehousing has added 
104,000 jobs since a recent employment low in February, with couriers and messengers (+71,000) 
contributing most of the gain. 
Manufacturing employment continued to trend up in October (+19,000) and has increased by 101,000 
since a recent low in December 2025. In October, job gains occurred in computer and electronic 
product manufacturing (+7,000), machinery manufacturing (+4,000), and primary metal manufacturing 
(+4,000). 
Employment showed little change over the month in other major industries, including mining, 
quarrying, and oil and gas extraction; construction; wholesale trade; retail trade; information; 
financial activities; social assistance; leisure and hospitality; other services; and government. 
In October, average hourly earnings for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls increased by 14 
cents, or 0.4 percent, to $38.00. Over the past 12 months, average hourly earnings have increased 
by 3.1 percent. In October, average hourly earnings of private-sector production and nonsupervisory 
employees rose by 12 cents, or 0.4 percent, to $32.75. (See tables B-3 and B-8.) 
The average workweek for all employees on private nonfarm payrolls remained at 34.4 hours in 
October. In manufacturing, the average workweek was unchanged at 40.5 hours, and overtime edged up 
by 0.1 hour to 3.1 hours. The average workweek for production and nonsupervisory employees on 
private nonfarm payrolls declined by 0.1 hour to 33.8 hours. (See tables B-2 and B-7.) 
The change in total nonfarm payroll employment for August was revised up by 53,000, from +133,000 
to +186,000, and the change for September was revised up by 31,000, from +29,000 to +60,000. With 
these revisions, employment in August and September combined is 84,000 higher than previously 
reported. (Monthly revisions result from additional reports received from businesses and government 
agencies since the last published estimates and from the recalculation of seasonal factors.)

 PRODUCER PRICE INDEXES - OCTOBER 2026
The Producer Price Index for final demand rose 0.3 percent in October, seasonally adjusted, the 
U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics reported today. Final demand prices advanced 1.4 percent in 
September and 0.4 percent in August. (See table A.) On an unadjusted basis, the index for final 
demand increased 6.5 percent for the 12 months ended in October, the largest 12-month rise 
since moving up 7.4 percent in November 2022.
Leading the October advance in final demand prices, the index for final demand goods increased 
0.5 percent. Prices for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent.
The index for final demand less foods, energy, and trade services rose 0.5 percent in October, the 
same as in September. For the 12 months ended in October, prices for final demand less foods, 
energy, and trade services advanced 4.9 percent.
Final Demand
Final demand goods: The index for final demand goods increased 0.5 percent in October following 
a 2.5-percent rise in September. Over 60 percent of the advance in October is attributable to prices 
for final demand goods less foods and energy, which moved up 0.5 percent. The index for final 
demand foods increased 1.3 percent. In contrast, prices for final demand energy edged down 0.1 
percent. For the 12 months ended in October, the index for final demand goods increased 10.2 
percent, the largest 12-month rise since advancing 10.5 percent in October 2022.
Product detail: Within the index for final demand goods in October, prices for basic organic 
chemicals advanced 3.9 percent. The indexes for fresh and dry vegetables; gas fuels; aeronautical, 
nautical, and navigational instruments; jet fuel; and processed young chickens also moved higher. 
(See table 2.) Conversely, diesel fuel prices fell 7.9 percent. The indexes for pork and for passenger 
cars also declined. 
Final demand services: The index for final demand services moved up 0.2 percent in October, the 
fifth consecutive advance. Three-fourths of the October rise can be traced to a 2.0-percent increase in 
prices for final demand transportation and warehousing services. The index for final demand services 
less trade, transportation, and warehousing advanced 0.2 percent. In contrast, margins for final 
demand trade services decreased 0.2 percent.
Product detail: Over 80 percent of the October increase in the index for final demand services is 
attributable to prices for truck transportation of freight, which rose 3.9 percent. The indexes for fuels 
and lubricants retailing; health, beauty, and optical goods retailing; food and alcohol wholesaling; 
hospital outpatient care; and traveler accommodation services also moved higher. Conversely, 
margins for machinery and vehicle wholesaling fell 4.2 percent. Prices for system software 
publishing and for airline passenger services also declined.

advanced 0.4 percent in October, the third consecutive rise. Leading the October increase, the index

For the 12 months ended in October, prices for processed goods for intermediate demand increased 
14.6 percent, the largest 12-month rise since jumping 17.2 percent in July 2022.
Product detail: More than 40 percent of the October advance in the index for processed goods for 
intermediate demand can be traced to prices for basic organic chemicals, which moved up 3.9

fabricated structural metal products, and prepared animal feeds also increased. Conversely, prices for

Unprocessed goods for intermediate demand: Prices for unprocessed goods for intermediate

Product detail: A major factor in the October decline in the index for unprocessed goods for

Exports, Imports, and Balance (exhibit 1)

Explanatory Notes
Goods (Census basis)
Data for goods on a Census basis are compiled from the documents collected by U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) and reflect the movement of goods between foreign countries and the 50 states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands, and U.S. Foreign Trade Zones. They include government and non-government shipments of goods and exclude shipments between the United States and its territories and possessions; transactions with U.S. military, diplomatic, and consular installations abroad; U.S. goods returned to the United States by its Armed Forces; personal and household effects of travelers; and in-transit shipments. The General Imports value reflects the total arrival of merchandise from foreign countries that immediately enters consumption channels, warehouses, or Foreign Trade Zones.
For imports, the value reported is the CBP-appraised value of merchandise—generally, the price paid for merchandise for export to the United States. Import duties, freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in bringing merchandise to the United States are excluded. The exception is exhibit 17a, which shows CIF import value. The CIF (cost, insurance, and freight) value represents the landed value of the merchandise at the first port of arrival in the United States. It is computed by adding import charges to the customs value and therefore excludes U.S. import duties.
Exports are valued at the f.a.s. (free alongside ship) value of merchandise at the U.S. port of export, based on the transaction price including inland freight, insurance, and other charges incurred in placing the merchandise alongside the carrier at the U.S. port of exportation.
Revision procedure (Census basis)
Monthly revisions: Monthly data include actual month's transactions as well as a small number of transactions for previous months. Each month, the U.S. Census Bureau revises the aggregate seasonally adjusted (nominal and real, or chained-dollar) and unadjusted export, import, and trade balance figures, as well as the end-use totals for the prior month. Country detail data and commodity detail data, based on the Standard International Trade Classification (SITC) Revision 4 and the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS), are not revised monthly. The timing adjustment shown in exhibit 14 is the difference between monthly data as originally reported and as recompiled.
For August 2026, unadjusted exports of goods were revised up $0.1 billion and unadjusted imports of goods were revised up $0.2 billion. Goods carry-over in September 2026 was $0.8 billion (0.4 percent) for exports and $0.4 billion (0.1 percent) for imports. For August 2026, revised export carry-over was less than $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent) and revised import carry-over was $0.1 billion (less than 0.1 percent).
Quarterly revisions to chain-weighted dollar series: For March, June, September, and December statistical month releases, revisions are made to the real, or chained-dollar, series presented in exhibits 10 and 11: the previous five months are revised to incorporate the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics' (BLS) revisions to price indexes, which are used to produce the real series and to align Census data with data published by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) in the national income and product accounts (NIPAs).
Annual revisions: Each June, not seasonally adjusted goods data are revised to redistribute monthly data that arrived too late for inclusion in the month of transaction. GDP (Advance Estimate), 3rd Quarter 2026
Real gross domestic product (GDP) increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the third quarter of 2026 (July, August, and September), according to the advance estimate released today by the U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA). In the second quarter, real GDP increased 2.2 percent.
The contributors to the increase in real GDP in the third quarter were increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased. For more information, refer to the "Technical Notes" below.
Compared to the second quarter, the acceleration in real GDP in the third quarter primarily reflected an acceleration in investment and an upturn in government spending that were partly offset by a downturn in exports. Imports increased more in the third quarter than in the second quarter.
Real final sales to private domestic purchasers, the sum of consumer spending and gross private fixed investment, increased 4.9 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 4.6 percent in the second quarter.
The price index for gross domestic purchases increased 3.0 percent in the third quarter, compared with an increase of 5.6 percent in the second quarter. The personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index increased 2.1 percent, compared with an increase of 5.0 percent, and the PCE price index, excluding food and energy increased 2.5 percent, compared with an increase of 3.3 percent.

Technical Notes
Sources of change for real GDP
Real GDP increased at an annual rate of 3.4 percent (0.8 percent at a quarterly rate 1) in the third quarter, reflecting increases in investment, consumer spending, and government spending that were partly offset by a decrease in exports. Imports, which are a subtraction in the calculation of GDP, increased.
More information on the source data and BEA assumptions that underlie the third-quarter estimate is shown in the key source data and assumptions table.
The increase in investment primarily reflected increases in private inventory investment and in equipment.
The largest contributors to the increase in private inventory investment were wholesale trade and manufacturing (both led by nondurable goods industries), based primarily on Census Bureau inventory book value data.
Within equipment, the increase was led by information processing equipment (mainly computers and peripheral equipment), based primarily on data for imports from the U.S. Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services report and the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September.
The increase in consumer spending reflected increases in both services and goods.
Within services, the increase was led by health care (mainly hospitals and outpatient services), based primarily on U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics’ Current Employment Statistics, and food services and accommodations (mainly purchased meals and beverages), based on Census Bureau Monthly Retail Trade Survey (MRTS) data.
Within goods, the increase was led by other nondurable goods (mainly prescription drugs), based on Census Bureau MRTS data.
Within government spending, the increase was more than accounted for by federal government spending, led by nondefense consumption expenditures. The pattern of nondefense spending primarily reflected sales of crude oil from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, based on data from the U.S. Department of Energy. Within the National Economic Accounts, sales are deducted from government consumption expenditures. In the third quarter, sales from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve were less than sales in the second quarter, resulting in an increase in consumption expenditures. Because the oil sold by the government is reflected as an increase in other components of GDP, there is no direct effect on GDP.
Exports and imports primarily reflected Census Bureau-BEA U.S. International Trade in Goods and Services data as well as the Census Bureau Advance Economic Indicators Report for September. The decrease in exports primarily reflected a decrease in goods (led by petroleum and related products). The largest contributor to imports was capital goods, except automotive.

 November 6, 2026 
U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela in July were highest since 2017 
Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Petroleum Supply Monthly 
In July 2026, U.S. imports of crude oil from Venezuela averaged 701,000 barrels per day (b/d), the most since May 2017, before decreasing to 655,000 b/d in August, according to data published in our Petroleum Supply Monthly. 
Crude oil imports from Venezuela started the year at 200,000 b/d and have steadily increased most months this year. Increased imports from Venezuela are supported by high crude oil demand from U.S. refineries because of high global refinery margins and the easing of U.S. government restrictions on purchases from the country. Many refineries on the U.S. Gulf Coast (PADD 3) are configured to process heavy sour crude oil grades, such as those from Venezuela. 
According to data from Vortexa, the majority of crude oil exports from Venezuela in 2025 were destined for China. In 2026, Venezuela has exported no crude oil to China, and the United States has instead been the largest single destination by volume for Venezuelan crude oil exports. 
U.S. crude oil imports from Venezuela stopped shortly after the United States imposed sanctions on state oil company Petróleos de Venezuela SA (PDVSA) in January 2019. In November 2022, the U.S. Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control granted Chevron waivers to resume exporting crude oil from its joint venture operations in Venezuela to U.S. Gulf Coast refineries; Chevron resumed these exports in January 2023. 
The U.S. government eased restrictions on PDVSA following the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro in January 2026 and took additional measures to authorize U.S. companies to invest in the country to increase Venezuelan domestic crude oil production.

 November 13, 2026 
Hydropower generation in the Southwest fell to record lows this summer 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Form EIA-923, Power Plant Operating Data 
Prolonged drought conditions affecting the Colorado River Basin led to record low hydropower generation this summer in the Southwestern electricity supply region, which includes Arizona, New Mexico, and small parts of Nevada and California. Hydropower generation from April through August 2026 was 19% lower than during the same period last year and 28% lower than the 10-year average, according to the latest data from our Form EIA-923 survey. 
Water elevations at Lake Powell and Lake Mead, which are formed by the Glen Canyon Dam and Hoover Dam, respectively, hit record lows. To be able to generate hydropower at the Glen Canyon Dam, Lake Powell should have an elevation of at least 3,490 feet, also known as the minimum power pool. At the end of September, this elevation reached 3,518 feet, less than 1% above minimum power pool. The Hoover Dam requires an elevation of at least 950 feet at Lake Mead, which by the end of September reached 1,038 feet, 9% higher than minimum power pool. The U.S. Bureau of Reclamation manages most dams across the Colorado River Basin. Seven states (Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, New Mexico, Utah, and Wyoming) depend on the river for hydropower generation and for other water supply needs. 
To mitigate the risk of Lake Powell’s water elevation falling below the minimum power pool, water was released from Flaming Gorge, a reservoir located in the Upper Colorado River Basin. Additionally, water releases from Lake Powell were reduced to maintain an elevation of at least 3,510 feet given the most probable water inflows. 
However, lower water releases from Lake Powell could also impact water elevation downstream at Lake Mead, in turn affecting hydropower generation at the Hoover Dam. To address this possibility, the Department of the Interior decided to reduce the collective water consumption of California, Arizona, and Nevada by 1.25 million acre-feet each year over the next two years. 
 Data source: U.S. Energy Information Administration, Short-Term Energy Outlook, November 2026 
We expect hydropower generation in the Southwest will total 6.13 billion kilowatthours (BkWh) in 2026 in our November Short-Term Energy Outlook (STEO), 9% lower than last year and 24% lower than the 10-year average. In 2027, we expect hydropower generation in the Southwest to total 6.1 BkWh, 0.5% lower than this year. This year’s El Niño could bring more precipitation than normal, providing some drought relief and improving the hydropower generation forecast in the region. However, one good water year likely won't eliminate the effects of multiple years of water scarcity. 
According to the STEO, hydropower generation in the Southwest is expected to account for about 4% of the region's generation mix in 2026. That share has declined from a peak of 8% in 2011.
